newsitem.title: USA: Lawsuit filed vs Orange County, Calif 'bailout'.
newsitem.headline: Lawsuit filed vs Orange County, Calif 'bailout'.

text.p: A taxpayer lawsuit was filed on Wednesday against Orange County and the State of California, alleging that legislation passed to "bailout" the county from bankruptcy was unconstitutional.

The lawsuit, filed in Orange County Superior Court, seeks to stop Orange County from receiving any more of the nearly $600 million authorised by the legislation, according to Richard Fine, attorney for the plaintiffs.
The suit also demands that the county return funds it has already received, Fine said.
Fine said Orange County should never have sought this type of legislation, which diverts transit and other funds to help repay county bondholders.

"The special laws that were passed to bail Orange County out of its unique financial crises were designed to add unjustified, and we believe illegal, expense to the taxpayers," Fine said in a statement.
Fine cited the decision of a Los Angeles judge earlier this month in a similar case involving Los Angeles County and the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Richard Hubbell ruled that 1995 fiscal relief legislation that allowed Los Angeles County to take transit funds violated a provision of the state constitution that prohibits special statutes for the benefit of a county or city.
Fine said the Orange County legislation was "nearly identical" to the Los Angeles County legislation.
Orange County attorney Laurence Watson said he has yet to review Fine's lawsuit, but added: "I'm confident our legislation will withstand legal challenge."

The defendants named in the lawsuit included the State of California, state Controller Kathleen Connell, the County of Orange and its supervisors, the Orange County Transportation Authority and the Orange County Development Agency.

Orange County filed for protection under Chapter 9 of the federal Bankruptcy Code on December 6, 1994 after sustaining investment losses of more than $1.6 billion. The county emerged from bankruptcy earlier this year.
Initiated by a group called the "Committees of Correspondents," Fine's taxpayer lawsuit was titled "Steven White vs. State of California et al".
